wa.gloss: marks the topic — what the sentence is about

ga.gloss: marks the subject, and the object of 〜たい

o.gloss: marks the direct object — the thing acted on

ni.gloss: marks a destination, a point in time, or where something is

de.gloss: marks the means, or where an action happens

mo.gloss: replaces は or が to mean "too" or "also"

no.gloss: joins two nouns — possession, or one describing the other

e.gloss: marks the direction of movement — softer than に

to.gloss: joins nouns as a complete list, or marks who with

ka.gloss: turns a sentence into a question

made.gloss: marks the end point — "as far as", "until"

masu.name: polite non-past
masu.note: Attach ます to the verb stem: 止まり + ます. This is the form to default to with anyone you are not close to.

mashita.name: polite past
mashita.note: The past of ます is ました, on the same stem: 止まり + ました. です does not take it — it becomes でした.

masen.name: polite negative
masen.note: The negative of ます is ません, on the same stem: 止まり + ません. Nothing else in the sentence changes.

te-form.name: te-form
te-form.note: The connective form — it joins clauses and carries ている, てください and much else. Ichidan verbs take て on the stem; godan verbs change the ending by its final sound.

tai.name: want to
tai.note: Attach たい to the verb stem: 食べ + たい. It behaves as an adjective afterwards, and its object takes が rather than を.

potential.name: potential
potential.note: "Can do" — 払え, 使え. What the verb could act on becomes が rather than を, because the potential describes a state rather than an action.

scenarios.name: Bakery
scenarios.blurb: Asking for items, counting them, paying at the counter.

items.note: を marks the direct object — the thing you are asking for. は would make it the topic, which sounds like you are commenting on bread, not requesting it.

items.ans: クロワッサン|を|二つ|ください
items.note: The counter comes after を, not attached to the noun: ＸをNください. 二つ is the generic counter for small objects.

items.ans: メロンパン|は|あります|か
items.note: For existence questions the item is the topic, so は. か turns the sentence into a question — no rising intonation needed.
これ is 'this thing' on its own; この needs a noun after it (この パン).

items.ans: この|パン|は|甘い|です|か
items.note: 甘い is already an adjective — です only adds politeness, it never becomes 甘いだです or takes が here.

items.en: I want to eat something warm.
items.ans: 温かい|もの|が|食べ|たい|です
items.note: 〜たい takes が for its object, not を. Attach たい to the verb stem: 食べ + たい.
お願いします is softer than ください at the point of paying. Both are fine; the particle stays を.
で marks the means or instrument — by card, by train, in Japanese. 払え+ます is the potential form: 'can pay'.
Same frame as the first sentence. Once ＸをＹください is automatic, only the noun changes.
何 stays where the answer would go — Japanese does not move question words to the front.

scenarios.name: Train station
scenarios.blurb: Buying tickets, platforms, departure times, gates.

items.ans: 京都|まで|切符|を|二枚|ください
items.note: まで marks the end point of travel — 'as far as Kyoto'. 枚 is the counter for flat things: tickets, sheets, plates.

items.en: Which platform is the Osaka train?
items.ans: 大阪行き|は|何番線|です|か
items.note: 〜行き means 'bound for'. The whole phrase is the topic, so it takes は.

items.en: Does this train stop at Nara?
items.ans: この|電車|は|奈良|に|止まり|ます|か
items.note: に marks the point a motion verb arrives at or stops at. で would mean the action happens there, not that it arrives there.

items.en: What time does the next train leave?
items.ans: 次|の|電車|は|何時|に|出|ます|か
items.note: の joins two nouns: 次の電車, 'the next train'. Clock times take に.

items.ans: 指定席|を|お願いします
items.note: お願いします is the standard counter-window request. The object still takes を.
Location questions follow Ｘはどこですか — は, not が, because you already know what you are looking for.

items.en: Can I use this ticket tomorrow?
items.ans: この|切符|は|明日|使え|ます|か
items.note: 使え+ます is the potential form, 'can use'. Time words like 明日 need no particle.

items.en: I want to go to Shibuya.
items.note: 〜たい attaches to the verb stem: 行き + たい. に marks the destination; へ is also correct and slightly softer.
